questions.q: What does an MSTVF declare that an inline TVF does not?
options: A named, typed return table (e.g. RETURNS @Result TABLE (col type, ...))
A RETURNS TABLE clause with no column list
A WHILE loop, which inline TVFs are forbidden from using
A primary key on every column it returns
questions.explain: An MSTVF's signature is RETURNS @ReturnTable TABLE (columns) — a typed table variable the function body must fill itself.

questions.q: How does an MSTVF's body differ from an iTVF's body?
options: It's a BEGIN/END block that can contain multiple statements, filling the return table with INSERT
It must be exactly one SELECT, same as an iTVF
It cannot contain any SELECT statements at all
It can only call other table-valued functions, never query base tables
questions.explain: Unlike an iTVF's single SELECT, an MSTVF has a procedural BEGIN/END body that can use multiple statements, loops, or branches before a bare RETURN;.

questions.q: What is the real, well-known tradeoff of using an MSTVF instead of an iTVF?
options: MSTVFs have historically had worse cardinality estimation, which can lead the optimizer to a bad join plan
MSTVFs cannot accept parameters at all
MSTVFs can only be called from inside a stored procedure
MSTVFs are always slower to create, though just as fast to query
questions.explain: Because SQL Server can't see inside the procedural body the way it can an iTVF's single SELECT, it has often used a poor fixed row-count guess for an MSTVF, hurting downstream plan quality.

questions.q: What's the rule of thumb for choosing between an iTVF and an MSTVF?
options: Prefer an iTVF whenever a single SELECT can do the job; use an MSTVF only when the logic genuinely needs multiple statements
Always use an MSTVF, since it is strictly more powerful
Always use an iTVF, since MSTVFs are deprecated in SQL Server
It doesn't matter — the optimizer treats both identically
questions.explain: An iTVF should be the default because the optimizer can inline it; reach for an MSTVF only when you need real procedural logic a single SELECT can't express.

questions.q: How do you call a multi-statement table-valued function in a query?
options: In a FROM clause, exactly like an iTVF or a table
In the SELECT list, like a scalar UDF
Only via EXEC, like a stored procedure
It cannot be called directly — only from inside a trigger
questions.explain: From the caller's side, an MSTVF looks identical to an iTVF — you still write SELECT * FROM dbo.FnName(@value). The difference is entirely inside the function body.
